name: Make char cloth
summary: Natural fabric cooked without air until it will catch a single spark and hold it — the thing that makes flint and steel work at all.

materials.item: small metal tin with a lid
nail or knife tip to pierce the lid

steps.text: Punch ONE small hole in the tin's lid. One, not several.
Cut the fabric into palm-sized squares and pack them loosely in the tin. Loose, so gas can get out around them.
Set the tin in the coals. A jet of smoke will stream from the hole.
steps.why: That smoke is the fabric's volatiles being driven off. What is left behind is nearly pure carbon, which is what takes a spark.

steps.text: When the smoke jet STOPS, pull the tin out immediately.
Plug the hole with a twig or press it into earth, and let the tin cool fully before opening — twenty minutes at least.
steps.why: Air reaching hot char burns it to ash. Every impatient opening costs you the whole batch.

steps.text: Good char is uniformly matte black, holds its weave, and flakes rather than crumbles.

verify: A spark landing on it grows a spreading orange ring rather than a dot that dies.
Brown or stiff patches were undercooked — run those squares again. Grey powder was overcooked.
limits: Char cloth catches a spark; it does NOT make flame. It has to go into a tinder bundle to become fire — see `fire-tinder-bundle`.
It is fragile and it absorbs damp from the air. Keep it in the sealed tin and it lasts years; leave it out overnight in humidity and it will not take.
cautions: Synthetic fabric does not char — it melts, and the fumes are toxic. Burn-test an unknown fabric first: cotton turns to ash and smells of paper, synthetics ball up and smell of plastic.
The tin is hot far longer than it looks.
